column3: Near-verbatim parallel: a true divine promise, denied by most people who do not know, is affirmed through resurrection.
Historical outcomes made observable through travel support the focus's concern with missed evidentiary signs.
A messenger's denial of error does not clarify the divine promise or public ignorance.
Near-verbatim parallel: God's promise is true, yet most people do not know.
The opening defeat begins the immediate reversal whose promised fulfillment 30:6 confirms.
Human breach of what was promised contrasts with God's stated refusal to break His promise.
Its claim that most people do not know gives the focus's ignorance motif a resurrection-related setting.
The announced future victory supplies the immediate promised event confirmed in 30:6.
It directly affirms that God does not break the appointed promise, in a prayer for its fulfillment.
It explicitly forbids supposing that God will fail His promise to His messengers.
Successorship after an earlier people offers only a remote pattern of divinely ordered reversal.
The rebuke of a sexual wrong adds no promise, fulfillment, or knowledge parallel.
